entities.name: Algebraic Expression
entities.definition: A combination of variables, numbers, and arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation) that represents a value. Unlike an equation, an expression has no equality sign and cannot be "solved" — it can only be simplified or evaluated.
common_misconceptions: Expressions can be solved (they can only be simplified or evaluated)
3x means 3 × x but 3x² means (3x)² (it means 3 × x²)
x + x = x² (it equals 2x)
learning_objectives: Identify terms, coefficients, constants, and like terms
Simplify expressions by combining like terms
Expand and factor expressions
Evaluate expressions for given variable values
Apply the distributive property correctly
real_world_applications: Writing formulas for area, volume, perimeter
key_experiments: Algebra tiles: physically model expressions and simplification

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Angle
entities.definition: The figure formed by two rays (sides) sharing a common endpoint (vertex). Measured in degrees (°) or radians (rad). One full rotation = 360° = 2π rad.
common_misconceptions: Angle size depends on ray length (it depends only on rotation between rays)
Degrees and radians are the same (360° = 2π rad, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3°)
Negative angles don't exist (negative = clockwise rotation)
learning_objectives: Measure and draw angles using a protractor
Classify angles (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex)
Convert between degrees and radians
Identify complementary (sum = 90°) and supplementary (sum = 180°) angles
Use angle properties: vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding
real_world_applications: Optics (angle of incidence = angle of reflection)
key_experiments: Protractor practice: measure angles in everyday objects

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Area
entities.definition: The measure of the size of a two-dimensional surface or region. Measured in square units. The amount of space enclosed within a boundary.
entities.equation: Rectangle: A = l × w  |  Triangle: A = ½ × b × h  |  Circle: A = πr²
common_misconceptions: Area and perimeter are the same (perimeter is boundary length, area is enclosed space)
Larger perimeter always means larger area (a long thin rectangle can have large perimeter but small area)
Area units don't need to be squared (they must: cm², m², km²)
learning_objectives: Calculate area of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapezoids, circles
Find area of composite shapes by decomposition
Convert between area units (1 m² = 10,000 cm²)
Solve real-world problems (flooring, painting, land area)
key_experiments: Grid paper: count squares to find area of irregular shapes

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Arithmetic Sequence
entities.definition: A sequence in which each term differs from the previous one by a constant amount called the common difference d, so aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d. The terms grow or decrease linearly, and the sum of the first n terms can be written compactly as Sₙ = n/2 (a₁ + aₙ).
common_misconceptions: Arithmetic and geometric sequences are the same (arithmetic adds a constant; geometric multiplies by a constant)
The common difference must be positive (it may be zero or negative)
learning_objectives: Identify the common difference of an arithmetic sequence
Write the general term aₙ from the first term and difference
Compute the sum of an arithmetic series
Detect arithmetic patterns in applied contexts
real_world_applications: Steady slopes: costs, savings, and distances that increase by a fixed step
Scheduling and stacking arrangements with uniform increments
key_experiments: Stack identical objects one row atop another to generate linear-step counts

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Circle
entities.definition: The set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance (radius) from a fixed point (center). Key elements: radius (r), diameter (d = 2r), circumference (C), area (A).
examples: Pizza: diameter = 12 inches → area ≈ 113.1 sq in
Unit circle: r = 1, C = 2π, A = π
common_misconceptions: Circumference and area formulas are the same (C = 2πr, A = πr²)
Diameter is half the radius (d = 2r, so radius is half the diameter)
π = 3.14 exactly (π is irrational; 3.14 is an approximation)
learning_objectives: Identify radius, diameter, chord, tangent, secant, arc, sector
Calculate circumference and area
Understand π as the ratio C/d
Solve problems involving arcs and sectors
Apply circle theorems (angle at center = 2 × angle at circumference, etc.)
key_experiments: Measure circumference/diameter of circular objects to approximate π

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Combination
entities.definition: An unordered selection of items taken from a larger collection, where order does not matter. The number of ways to choose r items from n distinct items is C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n − r)!), often written as a binomial coefficient (n choose r).
examples: C(4, 2) = 6: from {a, b, c, d} there are six two-element subsets
Choosing 3 members of a committee from 5 people gives C(5, 3) = 10
C(5, 2) = C(5, 3) by symmetry C(n, r) = C(n, n − r)
The coefficients of (x + y)ⁿ are binomial coefficients C(n, r)
common_misconceptions: A combination counts the same as a permutation (a combination ignores order, giving fewer arrangements)
C(n, r) counts selections with repetition allowed (it assumes distinct items and no repetition)
learning_objectives: Distinguish combinations from permutations by whether order matters
Compute combinations with C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!)
Recognize binomial coefficients in expansion
Use combinations in probability counting
real_world_applications: Selecting committees, teams, or samples where order is irrelevant
Lottery and sampling probabilities built on unordered draws
key_experiments: Form all handshakes among a small group and count the unordered pairs to match C(n, 2)

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Complex Number
entities.definition: A number of the form a + bi, where a and b are real and i is the imaginary unit with i² = −1. The complex numbers extend the real numbers so that every non-constant polynomial has a root, and are represented as points in a plane with a real axis and an imaginary axis.
examples: 5 is a real number and also a complex number with b = 0
The roots of x² + 1 = 0 are x = i and x = −i
common_misconceptions: Complex numbers are just numbers that 'cannot exist' in reality (they are structured quantities with a precise algebra and many applications)
Every quadratic needs two distinct complex roots (repeated roots and real roots are still possible)
learning_objectives: Represent complex numbers in rectangular form a + bi
Add, subtract, multiply, and divide complex numbers
Find conjugates and reciprocals
Plot complex numbers in the plane and relate them to vectors
real_world_applications: Alternating-current circuit analysis using impedance phasors
Signal processing and the study of oscillations in physics and engineering
key_experiments: Show that x² + 1 = 0 has no real root yet has two complex roots

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

historical.stated_by: Gerolamo Cardano (first recorded use); geometric interpretation by Wessel, Argand and Gauss
historical.where: Ars Magna (Cardano); geometric interpretations by Wessel (1797), Argand (1806), Gauss (1831)
historical.note: The term 'imaginary' was coined by René Descartes (1637). Cardano's Ars Magna (1545) records the first documented use of imaginary numbers in solving equations; the geometric interpretation was developed later by Wessel, Argand, and Gauss.

timeline.event: First documented use of imaginary numbers in Ars Magna
Formalized the complex-number field and its notation

entities.name: Continuity
entities.definition: A property of a function at a point when the function value equals its limit there: lim_{x→c} f(x) = f(c). A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of that interval, meaning its graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. Continuity is a prerequisite for differentiability and for many fundamental results of calculus.
examples: f(x) = x² is continuous at every real input
f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at 0 (no finite value or limit there)
f(x) = |x| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at 0
Piecewise functions often show jump discontinuities at their breakpoints
common_misconceptions: A function continuous at every point is necessarily differentiable there (continuity does not imply differentiability)
A removable hole (point discontinuity) means the whole function is unreliable (only that single point is affected)
learning_objectives: Determine continuity at a point by comparing the limit and the function value
Classify discontinuities as removable, jump, or infinite
State the intermediate-value property and the extreme-value theorem on closed intervals
Recognize that differentiability implies continuity
real_world_applications: Spline interpolation in computer graphics relies on continuous curves joining segments
Continuity assumptions justify modelling population size, position, and temperature as smooth trajectories
key_experiments: Trace graphs with breakpoints and holes to identify where continuity fails

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Decimal
entities.definition: A representation of numbers using base-10 place value, where a decimal point separates the whole number part from the fractional part. Each position represents a power of 10.
common_misconceptions: More decimal places means larger number (0.5 > 0.123 despite fewer places)
Adding zeros at the end changes the value (0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500)
The decimal point moves when multiplying/dividing by powers of 10 (digits shift, point stays)
learning_objectives: Read and write decimals using place value
Convert between fractions and decimals
Perform arithmetic operations with decimals
Round decimals to specified places
Compare and order decimals
key_experiments: Base-10 blocks: model decimal place value with physical manipulatives

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Derivative
entities.definition: The instantaneous rate of change of a function with respect to its variable; the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to zero. Written f′(x) = lim_{h→0} (f(x+h) − f(x))/h, the derivative gives the slope of the tangent line to the graph at a point.
examples: The derivative of a constant function is 0
The derivative of f(x) = 3x + 5 is the constant 3 (its slope)
common_misconceptions: The derivative is the value of the function at a point (it measures change, not the function value)
A function must have a derivative everywhere (functions can fail to be differentiable at corners or breaks)
learning_objectives: Compute derivatives using the limit definition
Apply the power, product, quotient, and chain rules
Interpret the derivative as slope of a tangent and as instantaneous rate of change
Find extrema, tangents, and intervals of increase or decrease using derivatives
real_world_applications: Velocity and acceleration as derivatives of position with respect to time
Marginal cost and marginal revenue in economics as derivatives of cost and revenue functions
Optimization of area, volume, profit, and other quantities
key_experiments: Approximate instantaneous velocity by averaging over shrinking time intervals

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Determinant
entities.definition: A scalar value computed from a square matrix that encodes geometric and algebraic properties of the matrix, such as whether its linear transformation is invertible. For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] the determinant is ad − bc. A zero determinant means the matrix is singular.
examples: For a 3 × 3 matrix the determinant is found by cofactor expansion
The determinant of an identity matrix is 1
common_misconceptions: The determinant is defined for any rectangular matrix (it is defined only for square matrices)
A non-zero determinant and invertibility are unrelated (a non-zero determinant guarantees an inverse)
learning_objectives: Compute 2 × 2 determinants directly and larger ones by cofactor expansion
Use the determinant to decide invertibility of a matrix
Relate the absolute determinant to signed area in two dimensions
Solve systems using Cramer's rule where appropriate
real_world_applications: Testing whether a system of linear equations has a unique solution
Computing areas and volumes from coordinates of geometric shapes
key_experiments: Verify that det maps a pair of vectors to the signed area of their parallelogram

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Exponential Function
entities.definition: A function of the form f(x) = a·bˣ where the base b is positive and not equal to 1, with x as the exponent. The function multiplies by a fixed factor b over each unit interval, producing constant relative growth (or decay) rather than constant absolute change.
examples: f(x) = 2ˣ doubles with each unit increase in x
f(x) = 3·4ˣ models a population increasing fourfold each unit
f(x) = (1/2)ˣ models exponential decay, halving per unit
f(x) = eˣ uses Euler's number e as the natural base
common_misconceptions: Exponential growth and linear growth are similar (linear adds constants; exponential multiplies by constants and grows far faster)
A negative base is allowed for every exponent (b must be positive so bˣ is real for all real x)
learning_objectives: Identify exponential functions and distinguish growth from decay by the base
Evaluate and graph exponential functions
Model repeated proportional change with exponential functions
Use the natural base e and convert between different bases
real_world_applications: Population growth, radioactive decay, and compound interest
Epidemiological spread and cooling laws governed by proportional change
key_experiments: Fold a sheet repeatedly to observe area halving and thickness doubling (exponential change)

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

historical.note: Euler formalized the natural exponential function e^x and the constant e. Earlier exponential ideas predate the formal function: Bombelli (16th c.) worked on iterative growth, and exponential processes were used in finance and astronomy before the 18th century.

entities.name: Fraction
entities.definition: A numerical quantity that is not a whole number, representing a part of a whole. Written as a/b where a is the numerator (number of parts) and b ≠ 0 is the denominator (total equal parts in the whole).
examples: 3/4 means 3 parts out of 4 equal parts
common_misconceptions: Larger denominator means larger fraction (1/8 < 1/4 despite 8 > 4)
You cannot add fractions with different denominators (you can, by finding a common denominator)
Multiplying fractions always makes them smaller (multiplying by a fraction > 1 makes it larger)
learning_objectives: Identify numerator and denominator
Simplify fractions to lowest terms
Convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers
Add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions
Compare and order fractions
key_experiments: Fraction strips or circles: physically combine and compare fractions

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Function
entities.definition: A relation between a set of inputs (domain) and a set of possible outputs (codomain) where each input is related to exactly one output. Written as f: X → Y or y = f(x). The function assigns a unique output f(x) to each input x.
common_misconceptions: Every equation is a function (x² + y² = 1 is not a function of x)
f(x) means f × x (it means 'f of x', the output of function f at input x)
A function must have a formula (functions can be defined by tables, graphs, words)
learning_objectives: Distinguish functions from general relations
Identify domain and range
Evaluate functions for given inputs
Understand function notation f(x)
Compose functions: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))
key_experiments: Function machine: input → rule → output, explore patterns

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
entities.definition: A theorem connecting differentiation and integration. Part 1 states that the derivative of the integral of f from a to x is exactly f(x); Part 2 states that a definite integral is evaluated by an antiderivative: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) whenever F′ = f. The theorem makes derivatives and integrals inverse operations.
entities.equation: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x)   and   ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
examples: Since F = x³ is an antiderivative of f = 3x², ∫₁² 3x² dx = 2³ − 1³ = 7
The area under f(x) = 2x from 0 to 4 is F(4) − F(0) = 4² − 0 = 16
common_misconceptions: The fundamental theorem applies only to areas (it links any rate of change to its accumulation)
Differentiation and integration are independent ideas (the theorem shows they are inverse)
learning_objectives: State both parts of the fundamental theorem of calculus
Use the theorem to evaluate definite integrals through antiderivatives
Explain how differentiation and integration are inverse operations
Apply the theorem to compute cumulative change from a rate of change
real_world_applications: Converting velocity into distance travelled, and acceleration into velocity
Relating rates (marginal measures) to accumulated totals in science and finance
key_experiments: Show that the area-accumulation function F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt has derivative f(x)

provenance.source: Standard content of calculus curricula; classical theorem (Newton, Leibniz)

historical.stated_by: Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (independent)
historical.where: Newton's early work; Leibniz's published formulation
historical.note: Developed independently by Newton (c. 1665-1666) and Leibniz (1670s; published 1693), giving rise to a priority dispute.

timeline.event: Early development of the calculus relating differentiation and integration
Publication of the fundamental theorem of calculus

entities.name: Geometric Sequence
entities.definition: A sequence in which each term is obtained from the previous one by multiplying by a constant called the common ratio r, so aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹. The terms change by a constant factor, growing exponentially when |r| > 1 and shrinking toward zero when |r| < 1. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.
entities.equation: aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹   |   Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)   (r ≠ 1)
examples: aₙ = 3·2ⁿ⁻¹ doubles each term from the first term 3
The infinite geometric sum with |r| < 1 converges: 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2
common_misconceptions: The common ratio is the difference between terms (it is the factor by which each term is multiplied)
All geometric sequences diverge (those with a ratio of magnitude less than 1 converge)
learning_objectives: Identify the common ratio of a geometric sequence
Write the general term from the first term and ratio
Compute partial sums of geometric series
Sum infinite geometric series when |r| < 1
real_world_applications: Compound interest, population growth, and radioactive decay
Bouncing heights and folding problems that change by constant factors
key_experiments: Halving a strip of paper repeatedly to observe a geometric decreasing pattern

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Integer
entities.definition: The set of whole numbers and their negatives, including zero: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... Integers extend natural numbers to include negative values and zero, enabling subtraction to be closed within the set.
common_misconceptions: Integers are only negative numbers (they include positives and zero)
Zero is positive or negative (zero is neither)
Subtracting a negative number always gives a smaller number (subtracting a negative adds its absolute value)
learning_objectives: Identify integers and represent them on a number line
Perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of integers
Understand absolute value as distance from zero
Apply integer operations to real-world contexts (temperature, finance, elevation)
key_experiments: Number line walk: physically step forward/backward to model integer addition/subtraction

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Integral
entities.definition: A quantity that accumulates a function over an interval: the definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx measures the signed area under the curve y = f(x) between a and b, while the indefinite integral is an antiderivative or a family of functions whose derivative is f. Integration reverses differentiation.
entities.equation: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx  =  F(b) − F(a)  where  F′ = f
examples: ∫₀² 3 dx = 6 (area of a rectangle of base 2 and height 3)
common_misconceptions: The integral is only an area (it also accumulates any quantity being accumulated by the rate f)
The +C constant is unimportant (it is essential: antiderivatives differ by a constant)
learning_objectives: Interpreting the definite integral as accumulated change and signed area
Computing integrals of elementary functions using antiderivative rules
Relating the integrand f to its antiderivative F via the fundamental theorem
Using integrals to compute areas and volumes
real_world_applications: Computing distances, work, volume, and total change from rates of change
Accumulating probability over an interval from a density function
key_experiments: Approximate area under a curve with rectangles (Riemann sums), refining the partition

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Irrational Number
entities.definition: A real number that cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers. Its decimal representation neither terminates nor repeats. Together with rational numbers, they form the real numbers.
common_misconceptions: Irrational means 'illogical' or 'unreasonable' (it means 'not a ratio')
All square roots are irrational (√4 = 2 is rational; only square roots of non-perfect squares are irrational)
Irrational numbers cannot be approximated (they can be approximated to any desired precision)
learning_objectives: Recognize that irrational numbers cannot be written as fractions
Identify common irrational numbers (π, √2, √3, e)
Approximate irrational numbers using rational numbers
Understand that the sum/product of a rational and irrational is irrational (if rational ≠ 0)
real_world_applications: Geometry (circle circumference = πd, diagonal of unit square = √2)
Exponential growth and decay (e in continuous compounding)
key_experiments: Geometric construction of √2 using a unit square diagonal

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Limit
entities.definition: The value a function or sequence approaches as its input or index approaches a given value. Written lim_{x→c} f(x) = L, a limit describes the behaviour of f near the point c without requiring f to be defined there. Limits formalize instantaneous change and underpin the derivative and the integral.
examples: lim_{x→0} (x² + 2x)/x = 2 (even though the expression is undefined at 0)
common_misconceptions: If f(c) is undefined, the limit does not exist (the limit depends on nearby values, not the value at c)
A limit must equal the function value f(c) (they coincide for continuous functions, but not in general)
learning_objectives: Estimate limits from tables and graphs of values
Evaluate limits by direct substitution, factoring, and rationalization
Distinguish one-sided, two-sided, and infinite limits
Relate the limit to the formal definition in terms of neighborhoods
Use limits to analyze the behaviour of functions at points where they are undefined
real_world_applications: Instantaneous velocity as the limiting average velocity over shrinking time intervals
Predict the behaviour of a model (population, price) as a parameter grows without bound
key_experiments: Zooming on a function graph to observe values clustering toward a single output

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Linear Equation
entities.definition: An equation in which the highest power of the variable is 1. In one variable: ax + b = 0 (a ≠ 0). In two variables: ax + by + c = 0. The graph of a linear equation in two variables is a straight line.
entities.equation: ax + b = 0  (one variable) |  ax + by + c = 0  (two variables)
common_misconceptions: All equations with x and y are linear (x² + y = 1 is not linear)
The slope is always the coefficient of x (only in y = mx + b form)
Parallel lines have the same y-intercept (they have the same slope, different intercepts)
learning_objectives: Solve linear equations in one variable
Graph linear equations in two variables
Find slope and intercepts from equations and graphs
Convert between standard, slope-intercept, and point-slope forms
Solve systems of two linear equations (substitution, elimination, graphical)
real_world_applications: Supply and demand curves in economics
key_experiments: Graphing with technology: explore how slope and intercept change the line

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Linear Function
entities.definition: A function of the form f(x) = mx + b, where m (slope) and b (y-intercept) are constants. The graph is a straight line. The rate of change (slope) is constant everywhere.
common_misconceptions: Linear functions must pass through the origin (only if b = 0)
Slope is just 'steepness' (it's rate of change: Δy/Δx, with sign)
Parallel lines have the same y-intercept (same slope, different intercepts)
learning_objectives: Identify slope and y-intercept from equation, graph, or table
Graph linear functions
Find equation given slope and a point, or two points
Model real-world situations with linear functions
Compare linear vs non-linear relationships
key_experiments: Motion at constant speed: distance vs time graph is linear

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Logarithmic Function
entities.definition: The inverse of the exponential function: y = log_b(x) is the power to which the base b must be raised to obtain x, so bʸ = x. Logarithms convert multiplication into addition and satisfy identities such as log_b(xy) = log_b(x) + log_b(y).
examples: log_b(1) = 0 for any valid base b
common_misconceptions: The logarithm of a sum equals the sum of the logarithms (log(x+y) ≠ log x + log y)
Logarithms are numbers only for positive input (log of a non-positive number is undefined in the reals)
learning_objectives: Convert between exponential and logarithmic forms
Apply the product, quotient, and power laws of logarithms
Solve exponential equations using logarithms
Recognize logarithms as inverses of exponential functions
real_world_applications: The decibel scale and Richter magnitude as logarithmic measures of intensity
Growth and decay times (half-life, doubling time) solved logarithmically
key_experiments: Measure sound loudness in decibels and relate successive stages to multiplicative intensity

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

historical.note: Napier introduced logarithms in 1614; Henry Briggs developed common (base-10) logarithms from 1617.

timeline.event: Publication of Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio introducing logarithms

entities.name: Matrix
entities.definition: A rectangular array of numbers (or other entries) arranged in rows and columns, usually written within brackets. A matrix with m rows and n columns has size m × n. Matrices have defined operations — addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication, and transposition — and provide a compact representation for systems of linear equations and linear transformations.
examples: A column vector is a matrix with one column: [[1], [2], [3]]
Matrix multiplication is defined only when the inner dimensions match
An identity matrix I has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere
common_misconceptions: Matrix multiplication is commutative (in general AB ≠ BA)
A number times a matrix equals the matrix times an added constant (scalar multiplication multiplies every entry)
learning_objectives: Identify the size and entries of a matrix
Add, subtract, and scalar-multiply matrices
Multiply matrices and understand the dimension requirement
Represent systems of linear equations and transformations with matrices
real_world_applications: Computer graphics transformations (rotation, scaling, translation) encoded as matrices
Organizing and solving systems in economics, statistics, and engineering
key_experiments: Encode a rotations and scalings on a shape by multiplying column vectors by matrices

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

historical.where: 'A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices'
historical.note: Cayley formalized the theory of matrices in 1858. Earlier matrix-like techniques existed, notably Gauss's elimination method for solving linear systems (c. early 1800s).

timeline.event: Elimination method for solving systems of linear equations (predecessor technique)
Publication of A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices, founding matrix algebra

entities.name: Mean (Arithmetic Average)
entities.definition: The sum of all values in a data set divided by the number of values. It represents the central tendency or "balance point" of the data.
examples: Daily temperatures over a week: sum of 7 values / 7
common_misconceptions: Mean is always one of the data values (it may not be)
Mean is unaffected by outliers (it is highly sensitive to extreme values)
Mean, median, and mode are the same (they differ for skewed distributions)
learning_objectives: Calculate mean for ungrouped and grouped data
Understand effect of outliers on mean
Compare mean with median and mode
Interpret mean in context
key_experiments: Balance point: find where a ruler balances with weights at data positions

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Median
entities.definition: The middle value in an ordered data set. If there are two middle values, the median is their average. It divides the data into two equal halves and is robust against outliers.
common_misconceptions: Median is the same as mean (they differ when data is skewed)
Median requires the data to be numerical (ordinal data also works)
Median is affected by outliers (it is resistant to outliers)
learning_objectives: Find median for odd and even number of data points
Find median from frequency tables
Compare median vs mean for skewed distributions
Understand median as 50th percentile
key_experiments: Human median: line up by height, find middle person

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Natural Number
entities.definition: The numbers used for counting and ordering: 1, 2, 3, ... Natural numbers are the most basic number system and form the foundation for all other number systems.
common_misconceptions: Zero is a natural number (in standard mathematics, ℕ starts at 1; some definitions include 0)
Negative numbers are natural numbers (they are not)
Fractions are natural numbers (they are not)
learning_objectives: Identify natural numbers and distinguish them from other number types
Understand the closure property of natural numbers under addition and multiplication
Recognize that natural numbers are well-ordered (every non-empty subset has a least element)
real_world_applications: Basic indexing in computer science (though 0-based indexing is also common)
key_experiments: Count physical objects to verify one-to-one correspondence with natural numbers

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Percentage
entities.definition: A ratio or fraction expressed as parts per hundred, denoted with the % symbol. x% means x/100 or x hundredths. Percentages provide a standardized way to compare proportions regardless of the whole's size.
examples: 25% discount means paying 75% of original price
common_misconceptions: Percentages above 100% are impossible (150% means 1.5 times the original)
A 50% increase followed by a 50% decrease returns to original (it gives 75% of original)
Percentage points and percent are the same (going from 10% to 15% is a 5 percentage-point increase, but a 50% increase)
learning_objectives: Convert between percentages, fractions, and decimals
Calculate percentage of a quantity
Calculate percentage increase/decrease
Solve problems involving profit, loss, discount, tax, and interest
Distinguish between percentage change and percentage points
real_world_applications: Finance: interest rates, discounts, tax, profit margins
key_experiments: Grid paper: shade squares to visualize percentages as parts per hundred

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Permutation
entities.definition: An ordered arrangement of a subset of items drawn from a larger collection, where order matters. The number of ways to arrange r items selected from n distinct items is P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!; arranging all n items gives n! possibilities.
examples: P(3, 2) = 6: from {a, b, c} there are 3 × 2 ordered pairs
The letters of a 4-token word can be ordered in 4! = 24 ways
Choosing a president, vice-president, and treasurer from 5 people gives P(5, 3) = 60 ordered outcomes
P(n, 0) = 1 for any n (the empty arrangement)
common_misconceptions: Permutations and combinations are the same (permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations ignore order)
Factorials count arrangements only when all items are distinct (repeated items require dividing out repeats)
learning_objectives: Distinguish situations where order matters from those where it does not
Compute permutations with the formula P(n, r) = n!/(n − r)!
Use the multiplication principle to count ordered outcomes
Translate counting problems into permutation statements
real_world_applications: Ranking outcomes and scheduling where order determines meaning
Cryptographic and lock arrangements built on ordered selections
key_experiments: List systematically all two-letter arrangements of a small set to verify the formula by counting

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Polynomial
entities.definition: An algebraic expression consisting of variables and coefficients, involving only the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and non-negative integer exponents. General form: aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ... + a₁x + a₀, where n is the degree.
common_misconceptions: Polynomials can have negative exponents (they cannot — that's a rational function)
Polynomials can have variables in the denominator (they cannot)
The degree is the number of terms (degree = highest exponent)
learning_objectives: Identify degree, leading coefficient, and constant term
Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials
Factor polynomials (common factor, grouping, special products)
Understand the relationship between factors and zeros
Apply the Remainder and Factor Theorems
key_experiments: Polynomial graph exploration: how degree and coefficients affect shape

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Probability
entities.definition: A measure of the likelihood that an event will occur, expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). P(E) = Number of favorable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes (for equally likely outcomes).
common_misconceptions: Probability can be greater than 1 or less than 0 (it's always 0 ≤ P ≤ 1)
Past outcomes affect future independent events (gambler's fallacy)
All outcomes are equally likely (often not true)
learning_objectives: Calculate probability for simple events
Understand sample space and events
Apply addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
Apply multiplication rule for independent events
Distinguish theoretical vs experimental probability
key_experiments: Coin toss experiment: experimental probability approaches theoretical as trials increase

historical.stated_by: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat
historical.where: Correspondence on the problem of points (dice problem)
historical.note: The mathematical foundations of probability began in 1654 through the Pascal-Fermat correspondence; Girolamo Cardano had earlier written on games of chance (Liber de Ludo Aleae, c. 1560s, published posthumously 1663).

timeline.event: Early work on games of chance (Liber de Ludo Aleae, published 1663)

timeline.by: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat
timeline.event: Correspondence founding the mathematical theory of probability

entities.name: Proportion
entities.definition: An equation stating that two ratios are equal. If a:b = c:d, then a, b, c, d are in proportion. This means a/b = c/d, or equivalently a×d = b×c (cross-multiplication).
examples: If 3 apples cost $6, then 5 apples cost $10: 3/6 = 5/10
Map scale: 1 cm : 5 km = 3 cm : 15 km
common_misconceptions: Proportions only work with whole numbers (they work with any real numbers)
Cross-multiplication works for any equation (only for proportions a/b = c/d)
If a:b = c:d then a:c = b:d (this is true, but must be derived correctly)
learning_objectives: Set up and solve proportions
Apply cross-multiplication correctly
Distinguish direct and inverse proportion
Solve real-world problems using proportions
key_experiments: Shadow measurement: use similar triangles to find height of tall objects

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Pythagorean Theorem
entities.definition: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides. This is one of the most fundamental theorems in geometry, connecting algebra and geometry.
examples: Ladder problem: base 3m from wall, top 4m high → ladder = 5m
Diagonal of rectangle: w² + h² = d²
common_misconceptions: Works for all triangles (only right triangles)
c is always the longest side (yes, hypotenuse is longest, but must identify which is c)
a² + b² = c² means a + b = c (false; √(a²+b²) ≠ a+b)
learning_objectives: State and apply the theorem
Identify right triangles using the converse (if a²+b²=c², then right angle)
Solve real-world problems (distance, height, diagonal)
Extend to 3D: distance in space = √(x²+y²+z²)
key_experiments: Rope with 12 equally spaced knots: form 3-4-5 triangle for right angle

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

historical.where: Traditionally attributed to the Pythagorean school (6th century BCE)
historical.note: The relation between the sides of a right triangle was known to earlier Babylonian, Indian and Chinese mathematicians; the attribution of a formal proof to Pythagoras is traditional and not directly documented.

entities.name: Quadratic Equation
entities.definition: An equation in which the highest power of the variable is 2. Standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0). Quadratic equations have at most two real solutions (roots), found by factoring, completing the square, or the quadratic formula.
common_misconceptions: All quadratics have two real solutions (discriminant b² - 4ac may be negative)
The quadratic formula only works for x (it works for any variable)
If a = 0 it's still quadratic (it becomes linear)
learning_objectives: Identify quadratic equations in standard form
Solve by factoring when possible
Solve using the quadratic formula
Understand the discriminant and its relation to number/type of roots
Relate roots to x-intercepts of the parabola graph
key_experiments: Ball throw: measure height vs time, fit quadratic model

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

historical.note: Old Babylonian scribes solved quadratic problems using procedures equivalent to the modern formula. Exact first authorship is unknown; the problem was later treated geometrically by Euclid and systematically by Al-Khwarizmi (9th century CE).

timeline.event: Solution of quadratic problems on Old Babylonian cuneiform tablets

entities.name: Quadratic Function
entities.definition: A function of the form f(x) = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0). The graph is a parabola. If a > 0, parabola opens upward (minimum at vertex); if a < 0, opens downward (maximum at vertex). The vertex form f(x) = a(x - h)² + k reveals the vertex (h, k).
entities.equation: f(x) = ax² + bx + c  |  f(x) = a(x - h)² + k
common_misconceptions: The vertex is always at x = 0 (only if b = 0)
All parabolas have two x-intercepts (discriminant may be negative)
The coefficient a only affects width (it also affects direction and vertex position)
learning_objectives: Identify vertex, axis of symmetry, direction of opening
Convert between standard and vertex form (completing the square)
Find x-intercepts (roots) and y-intercept
Graph quadratic functions
Solve optimization problems (max/min of quadratic)
key_experiments: Ball launch: video analysis to get quadratic height model

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Ratio
entities.definition: A comparison of two quantities by division, expressed as a:b or a/b. Ratios describe the relative size of two quantities without requiring a common unit (unlike percentages which are always per hundred).
examples: Classroom with 12 boys and 18 girls: ratio 12:18 = 2:3
Map scale 1:50000 means 1 unit on map = 50000 units in reality
Recipe ratio: 2 cups flour : 1 cup sugar
common_misconceptions: Ratios and fractions are the same (3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5 of total, not 3/2)
Ratio order doesn't matter (2:3 ≠ 3:2)
Ratios must be whole numbers (can be decimals: 1.5:1)
learning_objectives: Write and simplify ratios
Divide a quantity in a given ratio
Solve problems involving direct proportion using ratios
Apply ratios to scale drawings, maps, and models
key_experiments: Scale model building: measure and scale down real objects

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Rational Number
entities.definition: Any number that can be expressed as the quotient p/q of two integers, where q ≠ 0. Rational numbers include all integers, fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals.
common_misconceptions: All decimals are rational (non-terminating, non-repeating decimals like π are irrational)
Fractions with large denominators are not rational (any integer ratio is rational)
0.999... ≠ 1 (it equals 1 exactly)
learning_objectives: Identify rational numbers in fraction, decimal, and percentage forms
Convert between fraction, decimal, and percentage representations
Perform arithmetic operations with rational numbers
Understand density: between any two rationals there is another rational
real_world_applications: Probability (ratios of favorable to total outcomes)
key_experiments: Long division exploration: discover which fractions terminate and which repeat

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Sequence
entities.definition: An ordered list of terms a₁, a₂, a₃, … in which a formula or rule assigns a term to each index n (usually a natural number). Sequences are functions whose domain is a set of consecutive integers, and they are classified by their patterns into types such as arithmetic and geometric sequences.
examples: The Fibonacci-like rule aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ defines 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …
common_misconceptions: A sequence is the same as its set of values (a sequence preserves order and repetition, a set does not)
Every sequence has a single obvious formula (many rules may fit finitely many terms)
learning_objectives: Distinguish sequences from general sets and identify their index domains
Generate terms from an explicit formula or a recurrence
Classify sequences as arithmetic, geometric, or other
Find the sum of a sequence via series
real_world_applications: Numbering of discrete steps in algorithms and amortization schedules
Modeling populations, interest compounding, and iterative processes in discrete time
key_experiments: Construct patterns of matchsticks to generate and predict subsequent terms

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

entities.name: Standard Deviation
entities.definition: A measure of dispersion that quantifies how spread out a data set is around its mean. It is the square root of the variance; for a set x₁, …, xₙ it equals sqrt((1/n) Σ (xᵢ − μ)²) where μ is the mean. A small standard deviation indicates values clustered near the mean, and a large one indicates wide spread.
examples: The set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} has a small standard deviation
The set {1, 1, 10, 10} spreads far around its mean, giving a larger standard deviation
Standard deviation shares the units of the original data, unlike variance
common_misconceptions: Standard deviation and mean measure the same thing (the mean locates the centre; the standard deviation measures spread)
A larger range always means a larger standard deviation is needed in every set (range ignores order and clustering of values)
learning_objectives: Compute variance and standard deviation for a data set
Interpret standard deviation as a measure of spread around the mean
Compare data sets by their dispersion
Relate standard deviation to the normal-distribution model
real_world_applications: Assessing risk in finance through return volatility
Quality control, where the spread of measurements signals process variation
key_experiments: Generate two data sets with the same mean but different spreads and compare deviations

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

historical.where: Statistical lectures and writings on the root-mean-square deviation
historical.note: Pearson introduced the standard deviation in the early 1890s as the root-mean-square deviation, building on Gauss's earlier method of least squares.

entities.name: Triangle
entities.definition: A polygon with three edges and three vertices. The sum of interior angles is always 180°. Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and angles (acute, right, obtuse).
examples: Equilateral triangle: all sides equal, all angles 60°
Isosceles triangle: two equal sides, two equal angles
common_misconceptions: All triangles have a right angle (only right triangles do)
The largest angle is always opposite the longest side (this is TRUE)
Two triangles with same angles are congruent (they are similar, not necessarily congruent)
learning_objectives: Classify triangles by sides and angles
Apply angle sum property (180°)
Use Pythagorean theorem for right triangles
Apply triangle inequality (sum of any two sides > third side)
Identify congruent (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and similar triangles
key_experiments: Triangle construction: given 3 sides/angles, can you build it?

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Trigonometric Ratio
entities.definition: Ratios of sides in a right triangle relative to an acute angle. The three primary ratios: sine (opposite/hypotenuse), cosine (adjacent/hypotenuse), tangent (opposite/adjacent). Extended to reciprocal ratios: cosecant, secant, cotangent.
entities.symbol: sin θ, cos θ, tan θ
entities.equation: sin θ = opp/hyp  |  cos θ = adj/hyp  |  tan θ = opp/adj
common_misconceptions: Trig ratios work for any triangle (only right triangles, or use laws of sines/cosines)
sin θ = 1 means θ = 1° (sin 90° = 1, sin θ ≤ 1 always)
cos θ is 'cosine of θ' not 'cos × θ'
learning_objectives: Define sin, cos, tan for acute angles
Use standard angle values (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
Solve right triangles (find missing sides/angles)
Apply to angles of elevation and depression
key_experiments: Clinometer: measure angle to top of tree/building, calculate height

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Variable
entities.definition: A symbol (usually a letter) that represents an unknown or changeable quantity. Variables allow generalization of arithmetic relationships and the formulation of algebraic expressions and equations.
examples: In 2x + 3 = 7, x is the unknown variable
In A = πr², r is the variable radius
In y = 2x + 1, x and y are variables with a functional relationship
common_misconceptions: A variable has only one value (it can represent many values or an unknown specific value)
Different letters must represent different numbers (x and y can be equal)
Variables are only for algebra (they appear in formulas, functions, statistics)
learning_objectives: Understand variables as placeholders for numbers
Distinguish between independent and dependent variables
Use variables to express patterns and relationships
Evaluate expressions by substituting values for variables
key_experiments: Pattern generalization: use matchsticks to build sequences, derive formula with variable n

provenance.source: NCTM Principles and Standards / ICSE Mathematics Curriculum

entities.name: Volume
entities.definition: The measure of the three-dimensional space occupied by an object or enclosed by a surface. Measured in cubic units. Capacity refers to how much a container can hold.
entities.unit: cubic metre (m³), cubic centimetre (cm³), litre (L = 1000 cm³)
entities.equation: Cuboid: V = l × w × h  |  Cylinder: V = πr²h  |  Sphere: V = ⁴/₃πr³
common_misconceptions: Volume and capacity are the same (volume is space occupied, capacity is how much a container holds)
Doubling dimensions doubles volume (it multiplies volume by 8)
learning_objectives: Calculate volume of cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, pyramids
Convert between volume units (cm³, m³, L, mL)
Solve problems involving filling/emptying containers
Understand relationship between volume and capacity
key_experiments: Water displacement: find volume of irregular objects
